title: Defining RuleBooks
body: Defining RuleBooks The preferred approach is to create your own RuleBook that extends rulebox.models.RuleBook , with a method called defineRules() . In this method you define all the rules that apply to that RuleBook using the RuleBox DSL. title: Home
body: RuleBox RuleBox is a modern, intuitive, natural-language rules engine for BoxLang and ColdBox applications, based on the great work of RuleBook - ported over to BoxLang. Tired of classes filled with if / then / else statements? Need a nice abstraction that decouples rules from each other and from the rest of your code? title: The RuleBook DSL
body: The RuleBook Domain Specific Language The RuleBox DSL uses the Given-When-Then format, popularized by Behavior Driven Development (BDD) and testing frameworks (TestBox, Cucumber, Spock), and heavily inspired by RuleBox's Java counterpart, RuleBook . title: Facts & Results
body: Facts & Results Working with facts Facts are provided to rules via given() / givenAll() . In a RuleBook , facts are supplied when the RuleBook is run. The facts available to rules and rulebooks live in a struct, so they're passed by reference - even if, say, an immutable object is replaced, the perception is that the fact still exists and provides a named reference to a representative object. title: Auditing Rules
body: Auditing Rules Rule auditing tells you which rules fired and which didn't. A RuleBook tracks this in a RuleStatusMap . Give your rules a name so the audit trail is meaningful - otherwise you'll see the rule's internal UUID instead. title: Externalized Rule Definitions
body: Externalized Rule Definitions Every rule you've seen so far is written in BoxLang, using the RuleBox DSL. Sometimes that's the wrong place for a rule to live - business users want to tweak a threshold without a deploy, or the rules genuinely belong in a database table next to the data they govern. title: Thread Safety
body: Thread Safety RuleBook and Rule are transient (non-singleton) objects, and given() / givenAll() write facts directly onto the instance's own state. That means a single RuleBook instance is not safe to run() concurrently from multiple threads, or with different facts across separate calls - the facts and the rule status audit trail accumulate on that instance across every run() call. title: Error Handling
body: Error Handling A then() consumer that throws If a then() consumer throws, RuleBox records the rule as FAILED in the audit trail (see Auditing Rules ) before the exception is re-thrown to the caller.
